title: 2 Kings 5:1–14
context: 2 Kings 5:1–14 tells how Naaman, the honored commander of Syria’s army, is healed of leprosy. The Hebrew term for leprosy covered a range of serious skin diseases. A captive Israelite girl serving his wife points him to the prophet in Samaria. The king of Syria sends Naaman with a letter and rich gifts to the king of Israel, who tears his clothes and fears a pretext for war. Elisha sends for Naaman, but instead of coming out he sends a messenger telling him to wash seven times in the Jordan. Naaman is offended, but his servants persuade him, and his flesh is restored like a little child’s. The narrator notes that the LORD had given Syria its victories through Naaman. Arminian and Reformed readers share the main themes: God’s mercy reaches a Gentile enemy, healing comes through humble obedience to God’s word, and the faith of a little captive girl is part of the story. Jesus later points to Naaman’s healing (Luke 4:27).

verses.text: Now Naaman, captain of the army of the king of Syria, was a great man with his master, and honorable, because by him the LORD had given victory to Syria; he was also a mighty man of valor, but he was a leper.
verses.arminianNotes: Naaman is a great and honored commander, but he is a leper. Arminian readers note the striking statement that the LORD had given Syria victory through him, showing that God works in the affairs of nations beyond Israel, and they see Naaman’s disease as the need that will bring him to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and stress God’s sovereignty over the nations, since even Syria’s victories come from the LORD. Both traditions see the verse setting up a story in which a powerful outsider learns that the God of Israel is the only true God.

verses.text: The Syrians had gone out in bands, and had brought away captive out of the land of Israel a little girl, and she waited on Naaman’s wife.
verses.arminianNotes: Syrian raiders had taken a little Israelite girl captive, and she serves Naaman’s wife. Arminians see a young girl, taken from her home, who still remains faithful to Israel’s God in a foreign household, a quiet example of faith in hard circumstances.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and see God’s providence placing her in exactly the right household. Both traditions note that the story begins with the least powerful person in it, and they read her presence as part of God’s plan to show mercy to Naaman.

verses.text: She said to her mistress, “I wish that my lord were with the prophet who is in Samaria! Then he would heal him of his leprosy.”
verses.arminianNotes: The girl tells her mistress she wishes Naaman could go to the prophet in Samaria, who would heal him. Arminian readers see her compassion toward her captor and her simple confidence in God’s prophet as a model of faithful witness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note that her words are the first link in a chain that leads Naaman to confess the LORD. Both traditions see her faith as genuine and her witness as used by God, without making her a symbol beyond what the text says.

verses.text: Someone went in and told his lord, saying, “The girl who is from the land of Israel said this.”
verses.arminianNotes: Someone tells Naaman’s lord what the girl from Israel said. Arminians see her words taken seriously in the household, which shows how desperate Naaman’s situation was and how God can use a small witness to reach the powerful.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and read the verse as a simple narrative link. Both traditions see the message passing from the girl to her mistress to the king as part of the way God brings Naaman to Elisha.

verses.text: The king of Syria said, “Go now, and I will send a letter to the king of Israel.” He departed, and took with him ten talents of silver, six thousand pieces of gold, and ten changes of clothing.
verses.arminianNotes: The king of Syria sends Naaman with a letter to the king of Israel and with ten talents of silver, six thousand pieces of gold, and ten changes of clothing. A talent weighed about 66 pounds. Arminians see Naaman expecting that healing must be paid for, which the story will correct.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note the enormous value of the gifts. Both traditions see the scene preparing for Elisha’s refusal of payment in 5:16, which shows that God’s gift cannot be bought.

verses.text: He brought the letter to the king of Israel, saying, “Now when this letter has come to you, behold, I have sent Naaman my servant to you, that you may heal him of his leprosy.”
verses.arminianNotes: The letter asks the king of Israel to heal Naaman of his leprosy. Arminian readers see the Syrian king assuming that healing comes through royal power, a misunderstanding that the story will correct by pointing to God and his prophet.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note that the letter addresses the wrong person, since the girl had spoken of the prophet. Both traditions read the verse as setting up the king of Israel’s helplessness in the next verse.

verses.text: When the king of Israel had read the letter, he tore his clothes and said, “Am I God, to kill and to make alive, that this man sends to me to heal a man of his leprosy? But please consider and see how he seeks a quarrel against me.”
verses.arminianNotes: The king of Israel tears his clothes and asks whether he is God, to kill and make alive, suspecting that the request is a pretext for a quarrel. Arminians see a king who rightly knows that only God gives life, but who does not think to seek God’s prophet.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see irony in the king’s confession that only God can heal, while he acts without faith. Both traditions read the verse as showing Israel’s king at a loss, which makes room for Elisha’s word.

verses.text: It was so, when Elisha the man of God heard that the king of Israel had torn his clothes, that he sent to the king, saying, “Why have you torn your clothes? Let him come now to me, and he shall know that there is a prophet in Israel.”
verses.arminianNotes: Elisha hears and tells the king to send Naaman to him, so that he will know there is a prophet in Israel. Arminian readers see Elisha’s concern that God’s reputation be known, and they see God’s word stepping into the gap left by an unbelieving king.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and stress that the purpose of the healing is that God be known through his prophet. Both traditions read the verse as a turning point that directs attention from royal power to God’s word.

verses.text: So Naaman came with his horses and with his chariots, and stood at the door of the house of Elisha.
verses.arminianNotes: Naaman comes with his horses and chariots and stands at the door of Elisha’s house. Arminians see the display of rank and power, which contrasts with the humility Naaman will need to receive God’s gift.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note the picture of a great man waiting at a prophet’s door. Both traditions read the verse as setting the scene for Elisha’s unexpected response, which challenges Naaman’s expectations.

verses.text: Elisha sent a messenger to him, saying, “Go and wash in the Jordan seven times, and your flesh shall come again to you, and you shall be clean.”
verses.arminianNotes: Elisha sends a messenger telling Naaman to wash in the Jordan seven times, promising that his flesh will be restored and he will be clean. Arminian readers see a simple command that calls for trust and obedience, with healing promised to those who do as God says.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and stress that the power lies in God’s word, not in the water or the ritual. Both traditions see the command humbling Naaman’s pride and treat the number seven as marking completeness, without building further doctrine on it.

verses.text: But Naaman was angry, and went away and said, “Behold, I thought, ‘He will surely come out to me, and stand, and call on the name of the LORD his God, and wave his hand over the place, and heal the leper.’
verses.arminianNotes: Naaman is angry, because he expected Elisha to come out, call on the LORD, wave his hand over the place, and heal him. Arminians see pride resisting God’s way, since Naaman wanted a dramatic healing that honored his status.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse exposing the natural human desire to receive God’s help on one’s own terms. Both traditions read Naaman’s anger as an obstacle that God graciously overcomes through his servants.

verses.text: Aren’t Abanah and Pharpar, the rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel? Couldn’t I wash in them and be clean?” So he turned and went away in a rage.
verses.arminianNotes: Naaman asks whether the rivers of Damascus, Abanah and Pharpar, are not better than all Israel’s waters, and he leaves in a rage. Arminian readers see national pride added to personal pride, and they see Naaman close to missing the healing because of it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note that the point is not the quality of the water but obedience to God’s word. Both traditions read the verse as showing how close Naaman came to rejecting the gift.

verses.text: His servants came near and spoke to him, and said, “My father, if the prophet had asked you do some great thing, wouldn’t you have done it? How much rather then, when he says to you, ‘Wash, and be clean’?”
verses.arminianNotes: His servants ask whether he would not have done some great thing if the prophet had asked, so how much more when he says, "Wash, and be clean"? Arminians see God using humble servants to persuade Naaman, and they see the appeal to reason leading him to obey.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s grace working through the servants’ wise words. Both traditions note that, as with the girl in 5:2–3, God uses people of low status to bring Naaman to the healing.

verses.text: Then he went down and dipped himself seven times in the Jordan, according to the saying of the man of God; and his flesh was restored like the flesh of a little child, and he was clean.
verses.arminianNotes: Naaman dips himself seven times in the Jordan as the man of God said, and his flesh is restored like a little child’s. Arminian readers see healing following humble obedience, and the image of a child’s flesh suggests a fresh start.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and stress that the healing is God’s work through his word. Both traditions see the verse as the climax of the first half of the story, and both note Jesus’ reference to Naaman in Luke 4:27 as an example of God’s mercy to Gentiles.
